prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can’t get rid of useful things and nobody wants to pick them up, I keep forgetting where I lay my umbrella. I don’t leave footprints in the snow anymore, we haven’t had a war on domestic soil in so long I wonder if I still got it. Because once I had it. I heard about a boy who once tied a string to his brother, he tied his brother to the ocean and the ocean to the blackbird— from the ground all the birds look like blackbirds from the ground a Stealth Bomber looks like a spaceship. The aliens are coming, they walk through birthday parties and basically go unnoticed. And this is kind of how I go through life, once I heated up a spoon in the microwave the fish have so much mercury in them they spark. I was handed a bayonet from the Civil War and a copper penny corroded with rust. When they take the Statue of Liberty apart to clean her her neck explodes with a million little spiders. Meanwhile in a forest somewhere someone cut open my grandmother’s belly and filled it with bricks something is coming soon I keep a bucket of lambs blood by the front door.

outputs.L2: Useful items cling to me—I'm unable to discard them, and there's never anyone willing to take them off my hands. My umbrella? I constantly lose track of where I set it down. These days I leave no tracks behind me in the snow, and it's been such a long stretch since any battle was fought on our own land that I question whether I've still got the ability in me. Yet there was a time when I did. Someone told me a story about a young boy who fastened a piece of string to his brother, then bound his brother to the sea, and the sea to a blackbird—but viewed from below, every bird resembles a blackbird, just as a Stealth Bomber, seen from the earth, could pass for a spaceship. Extraterrestrials are arriving; they stroll right through birthday celebrations and hardly anyone notices them at all. That's more or less my own way of moving through existence. There was that time I warmed a spoon inside the microwave. Fish carry such heavy loads of mercury now that they throw off sparks. I received a Civil War bayonet as a gift, along with a copper penny eaten away by rust. Whenever they dismantle the Statue of Liberty for cleaning, her throat bursts open with a swarm of tiny spiders. And elsewhere, deep in some woods, a person sliced open my grandmother's stomach and packed it full of bricks. Something is on its way before long—which is why I keep a pail of lamb's blood waiting beside my entrance.

# Reflections on Loss, Perception, and Impending Threat

There are days when I feel weighed down by the accumulation of useless possessions surrounding me, objects that no longer serve any meaningful purpose in my life. Along with this material burden comes something more troubling: a fading sense of direction, a creeping suspicion that I have somehow lost abilities I once took for granted. I find myself wondering whether these skills have truly vanished, or whether I've simply forgotten how to use them.

From my vantage point here on the ground, everything above blurs into ambiguity. Perspective has a way of distorting perception, flattening the distinctions between things that should be entirely different. Birds and Stealth Bombers become indistinguishable shapes against the sky, their true natures obscured by distance and angle. What is natural and what is engineered, what is harmless and what is dangerous—all of it merges into a single, uncertain silhouette.

This uncertainty hints at deeper, hidden threats moving unnoticed through our everyday lives. I imagine aliens walking undetected through the most ordinary of scenes—strolling casually through a child's birthday party while everyone remains oblivious, absorbed in cake and celebration. The dangers are there, camouflaged within the familiar, waiting just beneath the surface of the mundane.

Everywhere I look, I see signs of decay, both environmental and historical. Fish swim through waters thick with mercury, their flesh contaminated by our carelessness. Pennies corrode in forgotten corners, their copper faces greening with age. Even the Statue of Liberty—that towering symbol of hope and freedom—stands crumbling, her promise eroding along with her structure. The rot is pervasive, touching nature, currency, and our most cherished ideals alike.

And so I wait, anticipating the arrival of something ominous drawing steadily closer. I prepare myself the only way I know how, returning to ancient, protective rituals. I keep lamb's blood by the door, marking my threshold against whatever is coming, hoping that this old gesture of faith might spare me when the threat finally arrives.

# Analysis of the Poem

This poem employs surreal, fragmented imagery to explore themes of decay, unease, and a pervasive sense of impending catastrophe. The opening images establish a world of neglect and abandonment—forgotten umbrellas left behind in unnamed places, corroded pennies whose value and shine have been eaten away by time and exposure. These are small, overlooked objects, yet they carry an outsized weight of meaning. They suggest a civilization that has misplaced its protections and allowed its currency, both literal and symbolic, to tarnish. The umbrella, an object meant to shield us from the storm, has been left behind precisely when it might be needed most.

The poem's ecological anxieties surface through the image of mercury-laden fish, a detail that grounds the surreal atmosphere in a recognizable dread about environmental poisoning. What should nourish us has become toxic; the natural world, contaminated by human industry, now threatens the very people who depend upon it. This corruption of the pure and life-giving deepens the poem's atmosphere of quiet horror.

Perhaps most striking is the vision of a spider-filled Statue of Liberty—a monument to freedom and welcome overtaken by webs and crawling things. This grotesque transformation of a national icon speaks directly to the poem's meditation on collective identity. The symbol meant to greet the huddled masses has become a hollow vessel colonized by decay, suggesting that the ideals it once represented have been abandoned, allowed to gather dust and cobwebs in the dark.

Through its disjointed associations, the poem refuses easy narrative or resolution, instead accumulating dread through juxtaposition. The reader moves through these images as through a nightmare, each fragment loosely connected to the next by mood rather than logic. This structural choice mirrors the alienation at the poem's heart—the sensation of moving through a world that has become increasingly foreign and foreboding, where familiar landmarks and objects have taken on sinister new dimensions.

The poem culminates in its most ominous image: lamb's blood at the door. This haunting final note carries deep resonance, evoking the biblical Passover, when blood marked the doorways of those to be spared from destruction. Yet here the image is stripped of its promise of salvation and left instead as a marker of terror—a sign that catastrophe is imminent, that death passes near. It suggests both sacrifice and the desperate hope of protection, while leaving unresolved whether that protection will hold.

Taken together, these elements convey a profound meditation on national anxiety and personal disquiet. The poem captures a moment of collective unease, in which the structures and symbols meant to offer comfort—money, monuments, shelter, nourishment—have all been corroded, contaminated, or abandoned. What remains is the haunting sense of a threshold moment, a door marked and waiting, and the deep alienation of a speaker moving through a landscape that no longer feels like home.

# The Rise of the Stealth Bomber

Stealth bombers represent one of the most remarkable achievements in modern military aviation, and they exist **because** nations sought a way to penetrate enemy defenses undetected. The development of these aircraft revolutionized aerial warfare by combining advanced technology with strategic necessity.

## Why Stealth Technology Emerged

The primary reason stealth bombers were created is rooted in the constant arms race between offensive and defensive military capabilities. As radar systems became increasingly sophisticated, traditional aircraft grew more vulnerable to detection and interception. Military planners needed a solution, and the answer came in the form of stealth technology.

**Because** conventional bombers could be easily spotted on radar screens, engineers focused on reducing an aircraft's radar cross-section. This led to the distinctive designs we see today, where every angle and surface is carefully engineered to deflect radar waves away from their source.

## How Stealth Bombers Work

A stealth bomber achieves its near-invisibility through several key features:

- **Special coatings** that absorb radar signals rather than reflecting them
- **Angular or blended shapes** that scatter radar waves in different directions
- **Internal weapons bays** that eliminate the radar reflections caused by externally mounted bombs
- **Reduced heat signatures** to avoid detection by infrared sensors

The famous B-2 Spirit exemplifies these principles, with its flying-wing design that appears almost otherworldly against the sky.

## Strategic Importance

The stealth bomber remains valuable **because** it can deliver payloads deep into contested territory while minimizing the risk of detection. This capability provides nations with a powerful deterrent and a flexible tool for responding to threats across the globe.

As technology continues to advance, stealth bombers will likely evolve further, maintaining their position at the cutting edge of military innovation for years to come.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem full of surreal, disconnected images about paranoia, memory, and a vague sense of impending doom.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Weather Inside the Telephone**

The clocks have been lying to me again, their hands folded in prayer or apology, and somewhere behind the wallpaper my grandmother is still counting the silverware, one two three, a fork missing since 1962, and this is how it begins, always, with the small theft that unravels the house. Listen: the refrigerator hums a frequency only the dead can dance to. I have been meaning to tell you about the men in the parked car but the car was never there, or it was there yesterday, or it will be there, idling in the tense that hasn't been invented yet.

Memory is a wet dog shaking itself in the hallway of my skull. Everything I loved is drying in the sun like photographs no one took. Did you leave the door open? Did you always have that face? The mailman knows more than he lets on—see how he touches each envelope like a confession, how the stamps are little windows into rooms I used to live in, and behind every window a lamp I forgot to turn off, burning, burning down the archive.

Something is coming. It wears the shape of Tuesday. It smells like the copper taste before a nosebleed, like the hush after a phone stops ringing. My teeth have been rehearsing their own funeral. The birds outside have organized. They perch on the wire in the exact configuration of a warning I can almost read, and the alphabet keeps slipping, and the letters rearrange into the name of the thing I am not supposed to say aloud.

I checked the locks. I checked the locks. I checked the locks and found my own hands strange, these tenant hands, these hands that signed a lease I don't remember on a body that keeps forwarding my mail to strangers. The ceiling breathes. The static in the walls is spelling out the hour of my erasure in a language of small collapses.

And still the kettle. And still the light through the blinds, sliced into the ribs of some patient animal. And still the sense, thin as a hairline fracture running through the whole afternoon, that I have been left here on purpose, a witness to a crime that hasn't finished happening, waiting for the knock, the knock, the soft insistent knock of everything I've ever forgotten coming home at last to be remembered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental piece of flash fiction in first person that jumps between odd American imagery—the Statue of Liberty, Civil War relics, aliens at birthday parties—without a clear narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
# Amber Waves

The Statue of Liberty has a headache. I know this because I've stood inside her crown, tourist-packed and sweating, and felt the copper thrum of her migraine, that green-oxide throb of holding one arm up for a hundred and forty years. Try it. Try holding a torch that long. Try meaning something that long.

---

My grandfather kept a Minié ball in a coffee can. Said his grandfather dug it out of a Georgia field, said it had been meant for someone's chest. Now it rolled around with buttons and a dead man's dog tags and the pull-tabs of a thousand Pabst Blue Ribbons. History reduced to things that clink. I used to shake the can like a maraca. The dead don't mind. The dead love percussion.

---

At Tyler's seventh birthday party the alien wouldn't stop staring at the piñata.

Nobody talked about it. That's the thing about the Midwest—you can seat a gray-skinned visitor between the balloons and the sheet cake and everyone will just pass the paper plates. Marcy's mom offered it a juice box. It declined with what might have been dignity. Its eyes were the color of a drained swimming pool in November.

The children swung the bat. Candy rained. The alien flinched at the violence of celebration.

---

Here is what I know about America:

It is a Minié ball in a coffee can.
It is a woman with a headache and a torch.
It is a stranger at your child's party who will not eat but will not leave.

---

The torch is closed to visitors now. Has been since 1916. Something about an explosion, German saboteurs, a pier called Black Tom that blew sky-high and rattled Liberty's raised arm loose forever. So she stands there, arm aloft, but you can't go up anymore. The best part is sealed. You climb and climb and then—a locked door, a rusted stairway, a *no.*

That's the most honest thing she does.

---

My grandfather died holding the coffee can. Not really. But I like to think it. I like to think he shook it one last time and heard the whole century rattle—the bullet, the buttons, the beer—and understood it was all the same metal, just melted and poured into different shapes of wanting.

---

The alien left before the presents. Walked out across the soybean field toward something none of us could see. Tyler cried, but not about that. Tyler cried because he wanted the bigger slice.

We are always crying for the bigger slice.

Overhead, something bright and patient waited, blinking, the way the torch would blink if anyone were still allowed to light it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem in the voice of a slightly unhinged narrator who feels invisible and senses something apocalyptic is coming.
counterfactuals.output:
# Transmission from the Vanishing

Nobody sees me at the bus stop anymore, which is fine, which is *fine*, because I've been practicing my disappearance for years now and I think I'm finally getting good at it. This morning the cashier scanned my groceries and looked straight through me to the fluorescent hum beyond, and I wanted to say *I'm here, I'm the one buying all these batteries*, but the words dissolved on my tongue like communion wafers, like promises.

Listen. Listen to me. The birds have been flying wrong. You wouldn't notice—you, with your appointments, your certainties, your faces that people actually *remember*—but I notice. I have nothing but time to notice. They circle counterclockwise now, the crows, unwinding something, and the light at 4 p.m. has gone the color of an old bruise, that yellow-green of *almost*, of *soon*.

I pressed my palm against the window last night and left no fingerprint. Do you understand what I'm telling you.

The radios know. Between stations there's a breathing now, a great patient inhalation, and I lie awake translating the static into scripture nobody asked me to write. *Blessed are the overlooked*, it says, *for they shall witness the end unblinded.* We ghosts, we background people, we the extras in everyone else's blockbuster—we'll be the only ones still looking up when it comes.

And it's coming. I've counted the dead streetlights (seven), the stopped clocks (three), the times my own mother said my name this year (once, and she got it wrong).

So I'm ready. I've been ready. When the sky finally splits its seam and pours out whatever it's been hoarding, I'll be right here at the bus stop, transparent and grinning, the last honest witness, waving at all of you as you finally, *finally* turn to look.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surrealist monologue that blends folklore, war, pollution, and domestic anxiety into a single rambling paragraph.
counterfactuals.output: The frogs stopped singing the year my mother learned to fold artillery into bedsheets, and I mean this literally, the way the river used to mean something before it turned the color of old pennies and refused to reflect the moon back to us like a good river should, like the river in Grandmother's stories where the water-woman braided drowned soldiers' hair into rope long enough to hang the sky, and now I can't stop thinking about the dishwasher, how it hums the same frequency as the sirens did, or maybe still do, I've lost the ability to tell the difference between an alarm and an appliance, between the smoke that means dinner and the smoke that means the neighbors are gone, and the folklore men, those dry old crickets who used to sit at the crossroads collecting teeth for luck, they've all migrated into the walls of my kitchen where they whisper that the tap water has a soul now, a small green trembling soul, and it wants to know why we boiled its cousins, why we poured the factory's black milk into its childhood, and I would answer but the baby is crying and the baby has been crying for a hundred years, a soft municipal wailing that the whole town has agreed to call weather, and somewhere a general is planting flags in a field of my grandmother's teeth while the frogs, the frogs, if they ever come back, will find nothing left to sing to but the shine of oil on standing water and the last unwashed plate balanced at the edge of the sink like a moon that never learned how to set.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, dreamlike poem that mixes childhood memories with dread, using images like blackbirds, Stealth Bombers, mercury-filled fish, and lamb's blood on the door.
counterfactuals.output:
# Passover in the Age of Falling Sky

I was six when I learned the door
could be marked—lamb's blood, thumb-smeared,
a signal to whatever passes over
in the night, hungry, counting.

The blackbirds gathered on the wire
like a sentence I couldn't read,
their bodies small black holes
punched in the afternoon.

Mother said don't eat the fish
from the reservoir, its silver flesh
gone quicksilver, its eyes
two beads of poisoned mirror—

but I remember the taste,
metallic as a held breath,
the way the Stealth Bombers
slid over the backyard,

black kites with no string,
folding the daylight
into origami dread,
soundless as the thing

that visits the unmarked houses.
I was six. I painted my finger
red with something, pressed it
to the glass, to the pillow,

to the soft place behind my ear
where I could feel the engines
before I heard them,
where I still can,

where the blackbirds are always
lifting, all at once,
into a sky the color
of a fish's dying eye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
